# Atlanta's flat street network: findings

*Generated by `python -m sf_flat_routes report`. Every figure is computed from the analysis outputs in this repository; see `validation_report.md` for the checks against known ground truth.*

## The headline

The street network modelled here is 5,712 km long, of which 5,254 km is walkable. It climbs an average of 17.0 m for every kilometre of street, which is rolling rather than steep: only 15% of it has a pitch of 10% or more anywhere along the block. Across all 1,260 ordered neighborhood pairs, on foot:

| Objective | Mean distance | Mean climb | Mean steepest grade | Distance penalty | Climbing avoided |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shortest (distance only) | 7.40 mi | 560 ft | 18.3% | +0% | 0% |
| Balanced | 7.79 mi | 479 ft | 11.5% | +5% | 14% |
| Flattest (minimum climbing) | 7.94 mi | 448 ft | 16.6% | +7% | 19% |
| Grade-averse | 8.72 mi | 482 ft | 9.4% | +18% | 13% |

**About 7% more walking buys about 19% less climbing.** That is the central result: the minimum-climbing route is on average only 7% longer than the shortest one, yet it avoids 19% of the ascent, and it takes the typical steepest pitch from 18% to 17%.

That is a smaller prize than in San Francisco, where the same analysis found 14% more walking buying 39% less climbing. The likely reason is the shape of the ground: San Francisco's hills are walls with flats between them, so a detour goes round. Atlanta is a plateau cut by creeks: almost every trip crosses a valley or two, every crossing costs the same descent and climb wherever it is made, and what a flat route can do is stay on the ridge longer and choose the shallowest place to cross.

The grade-averse objective is worth separating out. It ends up climbing slightly *more* in total than the flattest route (482 ft against 448 ft) while costing much more distance, but it holds the steepest pitch to 9.4% where the flattest route still allows 16.6%. Total climbing and peak steepness are genuinely different objectives, and a single definition of "flat" cannot serve both: minimising total ascent will happily send you up one short wall, and avoiding walls will make you climb a little more overall.

A note on the steepest-pitch column. It is the least reliable figure here: it is set by the single worst few metres of a route, and a lidar artefact or a short ramp is enough to move it (see the validation report). The climbing totals are sums over the whole route and are not sensitive to that.

### Flat means high

**Edgewood Avenue Northeast - Peachtree Center Avenue Northeast - Decatur Street Southeast - Atlanta Beltline Southeast Trail** (4.8 km, 1.8% mean gradient) is the most important flat corridor in the city, serving 277 ordered neighborhood pairs and avoiding 4.0 km of cumulative climbing in aggregate.

The pattern in the table is in its last column. The median street in Atlanta sits at 291 m; 8 of these 12 corridors (25 of 44 km) lie above it. In San Francisco the flat streets are the valley floors. Here most of them are ridge tops: Atlanta grew up around railways, the railways were laid along the divides because that is where the grade is easy, and the streets beside them (Edgewood and DeKalb, Marietta, Lee and Murphy, Whitehall and Peters) and Peachtree on its own ridge inherited the same profile. The low ground is the creeks, and nobody goes far along a creek without having to climb out of it.

## Passes, saddles and barriers

The question "how much climbing is unavoidable between these two parts of the city?" is a **minimax** problem, not a shortest-path one: what matters is the lowest summit you can possibly cross. Solving it over a minimum bottleneck spanning tree gives, for every pair of neighborhoods, the exact elevation of the lowest available crossing and the block on which it happens.

Across all 630 neighborhood pairs the lowest possible crossing averages 1002 ft and reaches 1041 ft at worst (Adamsville to West End). Only 35 distinct blocks in the whole city act as the binding constraint for any pair -- the city's real passes.

| Pass | Neighborhood | Lowest possible crossing | Pairs forced over it | Gradient there |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (unnamed path) | West End | 1018 ft | 184 | 4.9% |
| Lawton Street Southwest | West End | 1041 ft | 35 | 2.0% |
| Blake Avenue Southeast | East Atlanta | 1036 ft | 34 | 5.5% |
| Andrew Young International Boulevard | Downtown | 1031 ft | 33 | 0.4% |
| Richland Road Southwest | Oakland City | 1021 ft | 32 | 14.3% |
| (unnamed path) | Candler Park | 1020 ft | 31 | 8.9% |
| Mount Gilead Road Southwest | Southwest | 962 ft | 28 | 2.6% |
| Northside Drive Northwest | Kingswood | 943 ft | 22 | 7.6% |
| Mozley Place Southwest | Mozley Park | 1018 ft | 22 | 3.1% |
| Campbellton Road | Elmco Estates | 1010 ft | 21 | 3.6% |
| Ralph McGill Boulevard | Old Fourth Ward | 999 ft | 20 | 5.6% |
| Sunset Avenue Northwest | Vine City | 997 ft | 19 | 4.0% |

The single most consequential pass in Atlanta is an unnamed path in **West End** at 1018 ft. It is the binding constraint for 184 of the 630 neighborhood pairs, more than any other block in the city, and its gradient where it crosses is 4.9%: a pass is the lowest way over, not a steep one.

The passes are all high, between 943 and 1041 ft, and that is the other face of the corridor result. The ridges that carry the railways through the city are the Eastern Continental Divide and its spurs: rain on one side runs to the Chattahoochee and the Gulf, on the other to the South River and the Atlantic. A trip between neighborhoods on opposite sides has to get over that line somewhere, and these are the lowest places it can.

## The distance / climbing trade-off

For every one of the 1,260 ordered pairs, a single weight is swept from zero (pure distance) up to the minimum-climbing objective, tracing the frontier between distance, cumulative climbing and peak gradient. The useful question is where the knee is: how much detour buys how much of the climbing.

- **Almost no pair can halve its climbing** by any route: 1 of 1,260 can.
- **30% of pairs can shed a quarter of their climbing**, at a median detour of **8%**; 19% of all pairs can do it within a 10% detour.
- Taken to the flattest possible route, the median pair sheds **19%** of its climbing for a median **10%** more distance.

The frontiers are concave: the first fraction of extra distance removes most of the climbing that can be removed, and everything after that buys very little. That is the practical argument for the balanced objective over the purely flattest one.

## Walking is not cycling

The two networks are modelled separately. Atlanta has only 9 km of public stairways, which are part of the pedestrian network and excluded outright for bicycles, so the difference here is mostly one-way streets, which bind a bicycle and not a pedestrian, and stress weights: a protected cycleway counts as 0.85 of its length, and a trunk road such as Ponce de Leon Avenue, Moreland Avenue or Northside Drive as 1.9.

The flattest bicycle route averages 8.08 mi and 454 ft of climbing against 7.94 mi and 448 ft on foot.

## How much of this depends on the modelling choices?

Every figure above was recomputed with the whole pipeline rebuilt under 10 one-at-a-time changes to the elevation parameters and the choice of access intersection (`outputs/sensitivity.md` has the full tables).

| Finding | Baseline | Range across all perturbations |
|---|---|---|
| Flattest route: extra distance | +7% | +7% to +7% |
| Flattest route: climbing avoided | 19% | 19% to 20% |
| Grade-averse: mean steepest pitch | 9.4% | 8.8% to 10.0% |
| Corridor material shared with baseline (by length) | 100% | 85% to 99% |
| Lead streets of the top 12 corridors kept | 12 of 12 | 11 to 12 of 12 |
| Dominant pass | West End, 1018 ft | same location in 10 of 11 runs; 1018-1019 ft |
| BeltLine trip: excess climb, flat vs shortest | 37.1 vs 60.9 m | flat 36.3-37.6 m, shortest 60.9-61.3 m |
| Mattison Cove Northeast: steepest pitch | 23.8% | 23.3% to 25.6% |

The headline barely moves: the perturbation that shifts it most is **point_rank_1** (second-nearest access intersection), at 20% climbing avoided against 19% at baseline. The dominant pass is in the same neighborhood in 10 of 11 runs, and the flat BeltLine route wastes less climbing than the shortest in 11.

The corridors are where the model is least rigid, and it is worth being precise about how. The *street* that qualifies as corridor material is 85-99% the same by length, and the top corridor is Edgewood Avenue Northeast in every run; what changes is where each corridor is cut and therefore what it is called, most under **point_rank_2** (third-nearest access intersection, 85%). A handful of borderline streets drift in and out of the top twelve (Peachtree Road): these are real corridors whose rank depends on tenths of a percent of gradient, not artefacts, and they should be read as a tier rather than a ranking.

## What this analysis does not tell you

- **Elevation is the ground, not the street surface, and the ground of 2018.** The 1 m lidar DEM is bare-earth, so bridges and tunnels are corrected by interpolating across the structure, and streets passing under a deck are bridged across it. Anything built or regraded since the survey is measured as it was.
- **Travel is modelled on street centrelines.** Sidewalk and crosswalk geometry exists in the source data but is deliberately excluded: including it would represent every street two or three times and wreck the corridor aggregation. Pedestrian distances are therefore block-scale, not door-to-door, and nothing here knows whether a street has a sidewalk at all, which in parts of Atlanta it does not.
- **36 of 248 neighborhoods, one access point each.** The pair matrix runs between 36 neighborhoods chosen to cover all 25 Neighborhood Planning Units, each represented by a single street-network-weighted, intersection-snapped point. The headline averages are averages over those trips, which are long: 7.4 miles on average by the shortest route. They say what the terrain allows across the city, not what a typical errand looks like.
- **City limits only.** Decatur, Druid Hills, East Point, Sandy Springs and the rest of the metropolitan area are outside the network, so a route cannot leave the city even where the flat way round would.
- **No traffic, surface quality, signals or safety.** The bicycle stress weights are a crude proxy for road class, not a level-of-traffic-stress model, and nothing here accounts for signal delay, pavement condition or collision risk.
- **Bicycle facilities in the analysis are OSM-derived.** The explorer's bicycle and low-stress layers are inferred from OpenStreetMap tagging. The route finder's *prefer calm streets* uses the Atlanta Regional Commission's facility inventory instead, which is regional and coarser than a city bikeway layer.
